author: Maria Daskalaki
title: How to get a building permit in Crete: the complete 2026 guide
description: A step-by-step guide to the Greek building-permit process in Crete — documents, authorities, timelines and the most common causes of delay.

body.c: Every successful build in Crete starts long before the first excavator arrives. In Greece, building permits are issued electronically through the e-Adeies platform under the building-control framework of Law 4495/2017. The system is far more transparent than it was a decade ago — but the file you submit still depends on input from several authorities, and that is where most delays begin.
Step 1: Confirm what the plot allows

Before any design work, establish the rules that apply to the land: whether it lies inside or outside a town plan, the building coefficient, maximum coverage and height, setbacks, and the minimum plot size for building outside settlement limits. Out-of-plan rules in particular have been tightened repeatedly in recent years, so assumptions based on a neighbour’s house are not reliable.

c: Topographic survey tied to the national grid (HEPOS)
Title review and cadastral (Ktimatologio) registration
Zoning, coefficients and any special regulations
Road frontage and legal access

body.c: Step 2: Clear the special authorities

Depending on location, the file may need input from the Ephorate of Antiquities (archaeological zones are common in Crete), the forestry service (to confirm the plot is not classified as forest on the forest maps), the coastal authorities near the foreshore, and environmental services in or near Natura 2000 areas. These clearances often take longer than the permit itself, so we start them in parallel with design.
Step 3: Prepare and submit the permit file

The file includes architectural drawings, structural and MEP studies, an energy-performance study under KENAK, fire-safety measures where applicable, budgets, and the owner’s ownership documents. Licensed engineers upload it to e-Adeies, and the municipal building service (YDOM) carries out the review.
timeline
How long does it take?

For a straightforward residential project with a clean plot, the permit stage typically takes three to six months from a complete file. Where archaeological or forestry input is required, allow more. Hospitality projects add tourism-licensing steps on top.
The most common causes of delay

c: Title or boundary discrepancies discovered late
Missing or incomplete special-authority clearances
Design changes after submission
Unclear access or road-frontage status

body.c: The fastest permit is the one where the problems were solved before the file was submitted.
At Modera Group our in-house regulatory team prepares and tracks every step, so owners — especially those living abroad — never have to chase an authority themselves.

faq.q: Can a foreign owner apply for a building permit in Greece?
faq.a: Yes. Foreign individuals and companies can own land and build in Greece. You will need a Greek tax number (AFM), and in some border regions an additional approval for non-EU buyers.
Licensed engineers registered with the Technical Chamber of Greece submit the file on the owner’s behalf through e-Adeies.

author: Sofia Andreadaki
title: Construction costs in Crete in 2026: what a villa, hotel or building really costs
description: Indicative cost-per-square-metre ranges for residential, hospitality and commercial construction in Crete — and the factors that move the number.

body.c: “How much per square metre?” is the first question every owner asks — and the honest answer is a range. Material prices, labour availability, site conditions and the specification you choose all move the number. Below are the indicative ranges we use for early planning in Crete in 2026.
cost
What drives the cost

c: Site and foundations: sloping plots, rock and retaining walls add cost quickly.
Specification: natural stone, large-format glazing and bespoke joinery can double the finishes budget.
Building services: heat pumps, underfloor heating, solar and smart-home systems.
External works: pools, landscaping, driveways and boundary walls are often underestimated.
Access and logistics: remote or narrow-road sites raise transport and crane costs.

body.c: Where the money goes
For a typical premium villa, structure and envelope account for roughly two-fifths of the budget, building services around a fifth, and finishes, pool and external works most of the rest.
split
What is not in the price per m²

Land, VAT, design fees, permit fees, utility connections, furniture and contingency sit outside most per-square-metre figures. We recommend a contingency of 7–10% for new builds and 12–15% for renovations of older stone buildings.
How to protect your budget

Price the design while it is being developed, not after. At Modera our cost-control team issues an updated cost plan at each design stage, so decisions are made with the numbers on the table — and the final contract reflects a fully defined scope rather than a set of provisional sums.
Budgets rarely fail on site. They fail in the design stage, when nobody was pricing the decisions.

faq.q: Is it cheaper to renovate a stone house than to build new?
faq.a: Not always. Structural strengthening, damp remediation and working around existing walls can make restoration as expensive per square metre as a new build, though the character is often worth it.
No. The ranges shown exclude VAT and land. VAT treatment of new buildings in Greece has changed several times, so confirm the current rules for your transaction.

author: Eleni Papadaki
title: Developing a boutique hotel in Crete: from plot to opening day
description: What it takes to develop a boutique hotel in Crete — market, location, design, licensing and the construction timeline that gets you open for the season.

body.c: Greece welcomed a record number of international visitors in recent years, and Crete — with two international airports and a season that now stretches from April to November — is one of its strongest destinations. Demand has shifted towards smaller, design-led properties with character: boutique hotels, suites and villa complexes.
arrivals
Start with the guest, not the building

Successful boutique hotels are defined by a clear guest profile: couples seeking privacy, families wanting space, or travellers looking for gastronomy and culture. The profile determines key count, room mix, amenities and ultimately the building.
Location and licensing

Hotels in Greece are licensed through the tourism authorities, with an operating licence (Special Operating Badge) required before opening, and star classification following specific technical standards. Plot rules, access, water supply and wastewater treatment must all be confirmed at feasibility — they are frequent deal-breakers.

c: Zoning that permits tourist accommodation
Capacity of water, power and wastewater infrastructure
Accessibility and fire-safety requirements by category
Parking and service access for operations

body.c: Design that operates well

Back-of-house is where boutique hotels win or lose margin. Housekeeping flows, laundry, storage, plant rooms and staff areas need as much attention as the infinity pool. We design these with the operator from day one.
Build to open on time

Hospitality projects run to a fixed date: the season. We programme backwards from opening, procure long-lead items such as glazing, lifts and kitchen equipment early, and schedule commissioning and snagging well before the first guest arrives.
In hospitality, a three-month delay is not three months. It is a lost season.

Modera Group delivers hotels and tourism projects from feasibility to opening, working alongside investors such as Sivan Invest Group and the Harmony Fund who understand both the asset and the operation.

faq.q: How long does it take to build a boutique hotel in Crete?
faq.a: From feasibility to opening, two to three years is realistic for a new-build boutique hotel, including design, permits and licensing. Conversions of existing buildings can be faster.

faq.q: Can I start with villas and add a hotel later?
faq.a: Often yes, if the master plan, infrastructure and permits are designed for phasing from the start.

author: Katerina Vlachou
title: Greece Golden Visa and new-build property: what investors should know
description: How the Greek Golden Visa thresholds apply to property in Crete, and why building new can be a smarter route than buying resale.

body.c: Greece’s residence-by-investment programme — widely known as the Golden Visa — remains one of the most popular in Europe. Since the 2024 reform, the minimum investment depends on location, which has made the choice of property more strategic.
The thresholds in brief

c: €800,000 in Attica, Thessaloniki, Mykonos, Santorini and islands with more than 3,100 inhabitants — which includes Crete.
€400,000 in other regions of Greece.
€250,000 for specific cases such as converting commercial buildings to residential use or restoring listed buildings.
In most cases the investment must be in a single property of at least 120 m².

body.c: Rules change, and conditions on short-term letting and property use apply. Always confirm the current framework with a qualified lawyer before committing.
Why build new?

Buying land and building a new villa lets investors control quality, energy performance and design — and often achieve a better value per square metre than buying a finished resale home. New buildings must meet near-zero-energy standards, which lowers running costs and supports long-term value.
How Modera supports investors

We work alongside your legal and tax advisers to deliver the physical asset: land due diligence, design, permits and construction, with documentation prepared for the residence-permit file. Through our partnership with Sivan Invest Group, investors can also access structured opportunities and guidance on the Greek market.
The visa is the door. The property is what you live with for the next twenty years — build it properly.

faq.q: Does buying land count towards the Golden Visa?
faq.a: Land combined with the construction of a residence can qualify under conditions. Your lawyer should confirm how payments for land and construction are documented.

faq.q: Is Crete subject to the €800,000 threshold?
faq.a: Under the rules in force since 2024, islands with populations above 3,100 — including Crete — fall within the higher threshold. Check for any later changes.

author: Maria Daskalaki
title: Archaeology, forests and the coastline: the approvals that shape building in Crete
description: Why archaeological, forestry, coastal and environmental approvals matter in Crete — and how to plan around them from day one.

body.c: Crete has been inhabited for more than nine thousand years. That history is part of the island’s magic — and part of every developer’s due diligence. Alongside the building permit itself, four families of approvals most often determine what, where and when you can build.
1. Archaeological approvals

Large parts of Crete fall within zones of archaeological interest. In these areas the local Ephorate of Antiquities must approve works, and may require supervised excavation or trial trenches. Finds can change a layout; early engagement keeps the design flexible.
2. Forestry status

Greece’s forest maps classify land that may be treated as forest or woodland, where building is heavily restricted. Before buying, confirm the plot’s status and, where needed, obtain a certificate from the forestry service.
3. The coastal zone

Sea-view plots are prized, but the foreshore and beach zone are public, and construction near the coastline is subject to strict setbacks and controls. The demarcation line must be confirmed, not assumed.
4. Environmental approvals

Projects within or near Natura 2000 sites, and larger tourism developments, may require environmental assessment and approval of environmental terms. The scale of the project determines the category and the timeline.

c: Start special-authority checks during feasibility, not after design
Budget time for possible archaeological supervision
Treat coastline and forest status as deal-breakers to verify before purchase
Keep design flexible until clearances are in hand

body.c: In Crete, due diligence is not paperwork. It is design input.

faq.q: Does an archaeological find stop a project?
faq.a: Usually not permanently. Most finds are documented and the project proceeds, sometimes with layout changes. Major finds can lead to more significant constraints.

author: Sivan Menahem
title: Sivan Invest Group and Modera: turnkey real-estate projects in Crete
description: How the partnership between Sivan Invest Group and Modera Group gives investors a single, accountable route from opportunity to finished asset in Crete.

Two strengths, one process

We wanted investors to feel the same confidence on a site in Chania that they feel reading a well-run fund report.

author: Sivan Menahem
title: The Harmony Fund and institutional-grade development in Crete
description: How the Harmony Fund and Modera Group bring institutional standards of governance, reporting and risk control to development projects in Crete.

body.c: Crete’s real-estate market has matured. Larger hospitality projects, residential developments and mixed-use schemes increasingly attract investors who expect the governance standards of institutional capital. The Harmony Fund, working with Sivan Invest Group, and Modera Group share a simple aim: to bring those standards to the island’s construction sites.
What “institutional-grade” means on site

c: Independent cost plans and stage-gate approvals
Documented quality inspections at defined hold points
Monthly reporting on budget, programme and risk
Clear separation of design, cost and site responsibilities with one accountable lead

body.c: Aligning capital and construction

Development risk is mostly construction risk: delays, overruns and scope gaps. By involving the delivery team at the investment stage, the Harmony Fund and Modera evaluate opportunities with real construction data, not estimates borrowed from elsewhere.
timeline
A long-term view of Crete

Sustainable, well-built assets hold their value. Energy-efficient design, durable materials and buildings that respect Cretan landscape and heritage are not only responsible choices — they are sound investment decisions.
This article is for general information only and is not an offer or solicitation to invest. Investment opportunities are available only to eligible investors through the appropriate documentation.

author: Dimitris Manousakis
title: Rural plots in Crete: access, water, power and the infrastructure behind a great build
description: What to check before buying a rural plot in Crete — legal access, water, electricity, wastewater and the site works that make a project possible.

body.c: A rural plot with olive trees and a sea view is the dream of many buyers. The reality of building on it depends on infrastructure that is easy to overlook in the excitement of a viewing: access, water, power and wastewater.
Legal access comes first

Outside town plans, the plot’s frontage onto a recognised road is often a condition for building. A dirt track is not necessarily a legal road. Confirm the status before buying — it affects both buildability and the permit timeline.
Water and wastewater

c: Municipal supply, private borehole or storage tanks — each with different approvals and costs
Wastewater: connection to a network where available, otherwise an approved treatment system
Irrigation for landscaping and pools needs to be planned with water availability in mind

body.c: Power and telecoms
Distance to the nearest grid connection can change budgets significantly. We request network studies early and combine grid supply with rooftop solar and battery storage where it makes sense.
Earthworks and retaining structures
Crete’s terrain is beautiful and steep. Terracing, retaining walls and drainage protect the building and the landscape — and are frequently the largest single item in external works.
The view sells the plot. The infrastructure decides whether you can live there.
Modera’s infrastructure team delivers earthworks, roads and utility networks for our own projects and for private and public clients across Crete.

faq.q: Can I use a private borehole in Crete?
faq.a: Boreholes require a licence and are subject to water-resource limits that vary by area. Availability and quality should be checked before purchase.

author: Georgios Tsakiris
title: Why an owner’s representative saves money on construction projects in Greece
description: What an owner’s representative does, when you need one, and how independent construction oversight protects quality, cost and time.

body.c: Many owners, especially those living abroad, appoint a builder and hope for the best. An owner’s representative changes the balance: an experienced construction professional who sits on your side of the table and makes sure the contract is delivered as agreed.
What an owner’s representative does

c: Reviews contracts, specifications and bills of quantities before signing
Checks that work completed matches what is invoiced before payments are released
Inspects quality at key stages: foundations, reinforcement, waterproofing, services
Tracks the programme and flags delays early
Manages variations and keeps a written record of decisions

body.c: Where the savings come from

The largest savings rarely come from negotiating prices. They come from avoiding problems: paying for work not yet done, accepting defects that are expensive to fix later, or approving variations without understanding their cost.
split
When to appoint one

Ideally before the construction contract is signed. The contract is your strongest tool; a representative helps ensure it includes clear scope, payment milestones tied to progress, retention and defect obligations.
You would not sign a contract in a language you cannot read. A construction contract is a language of its own.

faq.q: Is an owner’s representative the same as the supervising engineer?
faq.a: Not exactly. The supervising engineer has legal duties under the permit. An owner’s representative focuses on your commercial interests — cost, quality and time — and can work alongside the supervising engineer.

author: Nikos Kalogerakis
title: Sustainable building in a Mediterranean climate: comfort, efficiency and value
description: How to design and build energy-efficient homes and hotels in Crete — orientation, shading, insulation, heat pumps and solar — in line with Greek NZEB requirements.

body.c: In Crete, the challenge is not winter cold but summer heat and intense sun. Sustainable buildings here are designed to keep heat out, let breezes in and generate their own energy — reducing running costs while increasing comfort and long-term value.
Design before technology

c: Orientation that limits west-facing glazing
Deep overhangs, pergolas and shutters for shading
Cross-ventilation and night cooling
Thermal mass from stone and concrete, protected by external insulation

body.c: Regulation: nearly zero-energy buildings

New buildings in Greece must meet nearly zero-energy (NZEB) requirements under the national energy-performance regulation, KENAK. An energy performance certificate is issued at completion. Well-designed projects in Crete can reach the top energy classes cost-effectively.
Systems that pay back

Air-to-water heat pumps, high-performance glazing, rooftop photovoltaics and solar water heating are now standard on our premium projects. For hotels, heat recovery and pool-heating strategies offer some of the fastest paybacks.
Water as a design priority
Rainwater harvesting, greywater reuse for irrigation and drought-tolerant Cretan planting reduce demand on an increasingly precious resource.
The most sustainable kilowatt-hour is the one the building never needs.

faq.a: Passive measures such as orientation and shading cost little when planned early. Active systems add upfront cost but usually pay back through lower energy bills and higher asset value.
